title: Multi-agent systems: when they're worth it, and when one prompt is enough
summary: Agent frameworks are powerful and easy to over-apply. A grounded take on when splitting work across agents earns its complexity — and when a single well-structured call wins.

sections.title: 1. Complexity has to pay for itself

blocks.text: Multi-agent architectures — a supervisor routing work to specialized workers — are genuinely useful, but they are not free. Every additional agent adds latency, cost, more places to fail, and a harder debugging story. Before reaching for an orchestration graph, the honest question is whether a single, well-designed prompt with good context would do the same job.

A good heuristic: if the task is one coherent transformation, keep it in one call. If it genuinely decomposes into steps that need different instructions, tools, or review — drafting versus critiquing, retrieving versus reasoning — then separate agents start to earn their keep.

items: Separation of concerns: a drafting agent and a reviewing agent hold different goals, and the tension between them improves output.
Tool specialization: one agent that only queries data, another that only writes, keeps each prompt small and reliable.
Human-in-the-loop checkpoints: a supervisor can pause the graph and wait for approval before anything irreversible happens.
Bounded loops: a critic agent can send work back for revision a fixed number of times, then stop.

sections.title: 3. Design for observability from day one

blocks.text: The moment you have more than one agent, you have a distributed system, and the hardest part becomes understanding why it did what it did. State that flows explicitly between nodes — rather than hidden in conversation history — is far easier to inspect, replay, and test.

# Explicit, inspectable state beats implicit chat history
class PipelineState(TypedDict):
    intent: str
    draft: str | None
    review_notes: list[str]
    approved: bool

# Each node reads and returns a partial state update,
# so every transition is loggable and replayable.

Always add a hard stop condition. Autonomous loops without an iteration cap are the single most common way an agent system runs up cost or spins forever in production. A bounded loop with a clear halt is the difference between a controllable tool and an unpredictable one.
